title: Proteins
summary: How amino acids are linked into polypeptides, why the variety of proteins is almost limitless, and how heat and pH disrupt protein shape. HL adds the four levels of protein structure and how form relates to function.

keyterms.definition: Monomer of proteins: a central carbon bonded to an amine group, a carboxyl group, a hydrogen atom and a variable R-group.
Covalent bond formed by condensation between the carboxyl group of one amino acid and the amine group of another.
An unbranched chain of amino acids linked by peptide bonds, made by ribosomes; one or more polypeptides form a protein.
An amino acid that the body cannot synthesize and so must be obtained from the diet; non-essential amino acids can be made from other compounds.
The three-dimensional shape of a protein, on which its function depends.
A change to a protein's conformation, e.g. by high temperature or extreme pH, that breaks the bonds holding its shape and usually causes loss of function.
R-groups differ chemically: hydrophobic (non-polar) or hydrophilic, and hydrophilic ones may be polar or charged (acidic or basic).
The sequence of amino acids in a polypeptide, which determines how it folds.
Alpha helices and beta-pleated sheets, stabilized by hydrogen bonds between amine and carbonyl groups of the polypeptide backbone.
The overall 3D folding of a polypeptide, stabilized by hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, disulfide bonds and hydrophobic interactions between R-groups.
Covalent bond between the sulfur atoms of two cysteine R-groups, helping to stabilize tertiary or quaternary structure.
The association of two or more polypeptide chains into one functional protein, e.g. insulin, collagen and haemoglobin.
A protein that includes a non-polypeptide component (prosthetic group), e.g. haemoglobin with its haem groups.
Globular proteins are rounded and often soluble, e.g. insulin; fibrous proteins are elongated, insoluble and structural, e.g. collagen.

questions.prompt: Which groups are attached to the central carbon atom of every amino acid?
options: A phosphate group, a sugar, a base and a hydrogen atom
Two carboxyl groups, a hydrogen atom and an R-group
An amine group, a carboxyl group, a hydrogen atom and an R-group
An amine group, a hydroxyl group, a glycerol and an R-group
questions.explanation: The generalized amino acid has –NH2, –COOH, –H and a variable R-group on one central (alpha) carbon. Phosphate, sugar and base describe a nucleotide.

questions.text: A peptide bond forms between the carboxyl group of one amino acid and the ___ group of the next.
questions.explanation: The –OH of the carboxyl group and an –H of the amine group are removed as water, leaving a –CO–NH– peptide bond.

questions.statement: Joining two amino acids to form a dipeptide is a hydrolysis reaction.
questions.explanation: Forming a peptide bond releases water, so it is a condensation reaction. Hydrolysis, which uses water, breaks peptide bonds during digestion.

questions.prompt: Which part of the amino acid structure differs between the 20 amino acids used to make proteins?
options: The amine group
The carboxyl group
The central carbon atom
The R-group
questions.explanation: All amino acids share the same backbone groups; only the R-group (side chain) varies, giving each amino acid its chemical properties.

questions.prompt: Match each part to its description.
questions.explanation: The amine and carboxyl groups are involved in forming peptide bonds; the R-group is left free to interact and determine folding.

questions.statement: Ribosomes link amino acids by condensation reactions to form polypeptides.
questions.explanation: During translation the ribosome catalyses peptide bond formation, a condensation, adding one amino acid at a time to the growing chain.

questions.prompt: Using the 20 amino acids, how many different tripeptide sequences are possible?
questions.explanation: Each of the three positions can be any of 20 amino acids, so there are 20 × 20 × 20 = 20³ = 8000 sequences.

questions.prompt: Order these from smallest to largest.
questions.explanation: Two amino acids form a dipeptide; many form a polypeptide; some proteins consist of more than one polypeptide chain.

questions.text: Because amino acids can be linked in any sequence and chains can be any length, the number of possible polypeptides is effectively ___.
questions.explanation: With 20 options at each position, the number of sequences is 20 to the power n, which becomes astronomically large even for short chains.

questions.prompt: How many water molecules are released when a polypeptide of 150 amino acids is made?
questions.explanation: A linear chain of 150 amino acids contains 149 peptide bonds, and each bond releases one water molecule.

questions.prompt: What is an essential amino acid?
options: One needed in larger amounts than other amino acids
One that cannot be synthesized by the body and must be obtained from the diet
One that is found only in animal proteins
One that is required for every protein the body makes
questions.explanation: Essential means essential in the diet: the body lacks the pathway to make it. Non-essential amino acids are still needed but can be synthesized from other compounds.

questions.statement: A vegan diet can supply all essential amino acids if it includes a suitable variety of plant protein sources.
questions.explanation: Individual plant foods may be low in some essential amino acids, but combining sources such as legumes and cereals provides all of them.

questions.text: Amino acids that the body can make for itself are called ___ amino acids.
questions.explanation: Non-essential amino acids can be synthesized from other amino acids or metabolites, so they need not be eaten directly.

questions.prompt: What happens to a protein when it is denatured?
options: Its peptide bonds are hydrolysed into free amino acids
Its amino acid sequence is changed
Its conformation changes because bonds that maintain its 3D shape are broken
It is converted into a lipid
questions.explanation: Denaturation disrupts the weaker bonds and interactions holding the 3D shape, so function is usually lost. The peptide bonds and amino acid sequence remain intact.

questions.statement: Heating a protein until it denatures breaks its peptide bonds.
questions.explanation: Peptide bonds are strong covalent bonds and survive heating; denaturation breaks the weaker hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds and other interactions that hold the shape.

questions.prompt: How does a pH far from a protein's optimum cause denaturation?
options: H+ or OH– ions hydrolyse the peptide bonds
The protein gains extra amino acids
The low temperature caused by acid slows molecular movement
Charges on R-groups change, breaking ionic and hydrogen bonds that stabilize the shape
questions.explanation: Changing H+ concentration alters which R-groups are charged, disrupting the ionic attractions and hydrogen bonds that hold the conformation.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.

pairs.right: Loss of 3D shape, usually with loss of function
Must be obtained from the diet
Chain of amino acids joined by peptide bonds

questions.explanation: Protein function depends on conformation, which depends on the amino acid sequence; denaturation destroys the conformation without changing the sequence.

questions.text: Proteins of bacteria living in hot springs have structures that resist ___ at temperatures that would destroy most proteins.
questions.explanation: Proteins of thermophiles have extra stabilizing bonds and interactions, so their conformation is not lost at high temperatures.

questions.prompt: What ultimately determines the conformation of a protein?
options: The sequence of amino acids, because R-groups determine how the chain folds
The number of water molecules released when it was made
The temperature at which it is stored
Whether it contains essential or non-essential amino acids
questions.explanation: The order of R-groups decides where bonds and interactions can form, so the sequence specifies the folded shape. Temperature can destroy a shape but does not specify it.

questions.prompt: Put the events in order as a protein is heated well above its optimum temperature.
items: Hydrogen bonds and other weak interactions break
Conformation changes and function is lost
questions.explanation: Heat adds kinetic energy; the increased vibration breaks the weak bonds that maintain shape, and the altered conformation can no longer function.

questions.prompt: In a globular protein dissolved in the cytoplasm, which amino acids are most likely to be clustered in the centre of the molecule?
options: Those with hydrophobic (non-polar) R-groups
Those with positively charged R-groups
Those with negatively charged R-groups
Those with polar R-groups
questions.explanation: Non-polar R-groups are excluded by water and cluster together inside the protein (hydrophobic interactions), while polar and charged R-groups face the surrounding water.

questions.text: Alpha helices and beta-pleated sheets are stabilized by ___ bonds between amine and carbonyl groups of the backbone.
questions.explanation: Secondary structure involves regularly spaced hydrogen bonds between C=O and N–H groups of the backbone, not the R-groups.

questions.prompt: Match each level of protein structure to its description.

pairs.right: Two or more polypeptides joined together

questions.explanation: Each level builds on the one before; the primary sequence ultimately determines all the higher levels.

questions.statement: Disulfide bonds are covalent bonds formed between the R-groups of two cysteine amino acids.
questions.explanation: Cysteine R-groups contain sulfur; two can form a strong covalent S–S bridge that helps hold tertiary or quaternary structure.

questions.prompt: Which interactions stabilize the tertiary structure of a protein?
options: Peptide bonds only
Glycosidic and ester bonds
Hydrogen bonds between backbone groups only
Hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, disulfide bonds and hydrophobic interactions between R-groups
questions.explanation: Tertiary structure depends on interactions between R-groups throughout the chain. Backbone-only hydrogen bonds describe secondary structure.

questions.prompt: In sickle cell disease one glutamic acid in a haemoglobin chain is replaced by valine. Why can such a small change alter the protein?
options: It removes a peptide bond, splitting the chain
The new R-group has different properties, changing which interactions form and so the conformation
It changes the number of polypeptides in haemoglobin
Valine cannot form hydrogen bonds with the backbone
questions.explanation: Glutamic acid has a charged hydrophilic R-group and valine a hydrophobic one, so the bonding pattern and shape change, making haemoglobin molecules stick together at low oxygen.

questions.statement: Haemoglobin is a conjugated protein because it contains non-polypeptide haem groups as well as four polypeptide chains.
questions.explanation: A conjugated protein has a prosthetic group in addition to its polypeptides. Insulin and collagen are non-conjugated: they consist only of polypeptide.

questions.prompt: Which amino acids would you expect in the part of an integral membrane protein that crosses the phospholipid bilayer?
options: Mostly negatively charged amino acids
Mostly polar amino acids
Mostly positively charged amino acids
Mostly non-polar amino acids
questions.explanation: The core of the bilayer is hydrophobic, so the embedded region needs non-polar R-groups to interact with fatty acid tails. Polar and charged R-groups face the aqueous environment.

questions.prompt: Match each protein to the feature that relates its structure to function.

pairs.right: Fibrous triple helix giving high tensile strength
Globular hormone of two disulfide-linked chains
Four chains, each with an oxygen-binding haem

questions.explanation: Collagen's three tightly wound chains resist stretching in tendons and skin; insulin's compact soluble shape fits its receptor; haemoglobin's haem groups bind oxygen.

questions.text: Rounded, usually water-soluble proteins with specific shapes, such as insulin, are called ___ proteins.
questions.explanation: Globular proteins fold compactly with hydrophilic R-groups outside, making them soluble; fibrous proteins like collagen are long, insoluble and structural.
